newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Jobs fall shows why Australian rates will not rise.
newsitem.headline: Jobs fall shows why Australian rates will not rise.

text.p: Unexpected weakness in Australia's labour market is compelling evidence against the case for Australia to follow the U.S. in lifting official interest rates, economists said.

Employment fell by 33,900 in March, well below median forecasts of a 13,500 rise, official figures released on Thursday showed. Of the 28 economists Reuters surveyed ahead of the data, none were expecting a fall. "It is telling us that we have a very weak labour market out there," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
The unemployment rate was 8.7 percent, as expected, but analysts said it was only saved from rising to over 9.0 percent by a large drop in the number of people in the labour force.
Perhaps the most worrying feature of the report was continued weakness in full-time employment.
Full time employment fell by 30,400 in March, and was down 54,500 over the past two months. Over the past 12 months, total employment has risen 90,000, but full time jobs have dropped by 6,000.
"This is a good reason why Australia won't be following in the footsteps of the Fed anytime soon," Henderson said.

The U.S. Federal Reserve lifted U.S. interest rates by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, and many economists expect a similar hike will follow the May 20 meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee.
That had led to some concerns that Australia's cash rate, which currently stands at 6.0 percent, would also have to rise.
However, analysts central case view had been that interest rates were on hold before rising in late 1997 at the earliest. After the jobs data, some were questioning that outlook.
"Will this still be the call if unemployment gets to nine percent and inflation falls to one percent?" Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.

Australia's inflation rate is expected to fall through the first half of 1997, and the Reserve Bank of Australia has said it expects underlying inflation, the focus of monetary policy, to stay in its two to three percent target band through 1998.
March quarter inflation data will be released on April 23.
Saving the unemployment rate from rising towards, or even over, nine percent from February's 8.8 percent was a drop in the participation rate, economists said.
The participation rate, which expresses the size of the labour force as a percentage of the population over 15, fell to 63.3 percent in March from 67.7 percent in February.
"If they hadn't had that fall in the particpation rate the unemployment rate would have gone through nine percent with no trouble at all," HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said.

However, economists were not yet convinced the weakness in the jobs data was enough to justify a rate cut to follow the three in 1996, despite inflation being expected to remain low for some time yet.

Future data might show the March fall to be a rogue figure, and other indicators such as retail trade and housing data were suggesting a stronger economy in 1997 which should help jobs growth, a lagging indicator of activity, they said.

"Nevertheless, today's data do serve to reinforce the notion that Australian and U.S. monetary policies are on divergent paths at present and that any rise in domestic interest rates is, in our view, very unlikely over the balance of 1997," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.
